newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Latin currency regimes face U.S. rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Latin currency regimes face U.S. rate rise.

text.p: After two years of warm glow nurtured by generous foreign capital, the currencies of four major Latin American countries may face a stress test if rising U.S. interest rates reverse the capital influx.

Economists and currency analysts anticipate no serious disruptions in the short term, but they say the Mexican peso could trade in a wider range and the Venezuelan bolivar could head into rougher waters, if U.S. credit becomes tighter.

Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and Venezuela, the four countries that together account for two-thirds of the Latin economy, are each pursuing a different currency regime with varying degress of rigidity and ties to the U.S. dollar.

The Argentine peso is pegged at parity with the U.S. dollar. Brazil's real moves in a band that is fixed periodically. Mexico follows a managed floating regime, and Venezuela sets a reference rate with targeted depreciation.
All four regimes have worked well in controlling inflation and boosting investors' confidence, which has prompted many market watchers to hail it as the dawn of a new era for Latin America.
But some analysts argue that the disadvantages of the regimes were not showing up because the weak balance of payments is supported by the flow of investment funds.

"In the rampant euphoria of 1996 and early 1997, any exchange rate policy you can devise will probably lead to a relatively stable, strong currency," said Ernest Brown, Latin America economist at Morgan Stanley.
The question arises how a currency can climb down without wreaking havoc on the economy, he said.
MEXICAN PESO

The Mexican peso, whose devaluation sent shock waves through emerging markets in December 1994, came under instant fire when U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan testified in Congress this month. His warning about soaring equity prices was seen as preparing financial markets for a monetary tightening. But in the second leg of his address, Greenspan tempered his hawkish tone.
The peso fell from 7.74 per dollar before the first part of the testimony to a low of 8.10 in the subsequent days. But the decline sparked no panic, traders said.

"The peso was slightly overvalued based on the inflation differential between Mexico and the U.S.," said Peter Allen, director of emerging markets research at BancBoston Securities, who saw the peso's weakening as on target.
The Bank of Mexico, which announced last month that it would sell $200 million of reserves if the peso falls by more than 2.0 percent in one day, did not intervene.

Robert Hodrick, Nomura Professor of International Finance at Columbia University's Graduate School of Business, said that while central bank intervention may smooth short-term volatility, it does not change the currency's value.
"It is the monetary growth in conjuction with the demand for pesos and what's happening to the monetary policy in the U.S. that determines the peso value of the dollar," he said.

Jaime Valdivia, vice president of emerging market fixed income research at Morgan Stanley, said he was "encouraged" that Bank of Mexico did not intervene. "It showed that the central bank was not concerned enough to implement the brake."
Mexico's economy grew a surprisingly strong 5.1 percent in 1996 and the improving credit fundamentals provide the underpinning of the country's currency, he said.
But the peso should slide to nine per dollar by year end, assuming an annual inflation rate in Mexico at 18.1 percent, according to his forecast.
BOLIVAR MORE PRECARIOUS
Compared to Mexico, Venezuela's bolivar is in a more precarious state, Valdivia said.
If the trend of deteriorating fiscal balance, loose monetary policy and stubbornly high inflation continues, the bolivar could see more turbulence ahead, he said.

Walter Molano, director of emerging market research at SBC/Warburg, said the bolivar is at least 20 percent overvalued, but the Venezuelan government has to maintain a strong currency to reduce inflation.
With a weak fiscal base and a shaky banking sector, the government has few alternatives to manage inflation, he said. "They have to rely on the exchange rate."
David Malpass, an economist at Bear, Stearns and Co, said Venezuela was following its neighbours' lead by keeping the currency stable against the dollar.
"It is a positive and dramatic departure from the past when the government printed money and had control over the exchange rate," he said.
But he refrained from predicting whether the government had the political will to pull it through.
"It is too early to tell," he said.
ARGENTINE, BRAZILIAN CURRENCIES LIKELY TO KEEP VALUE
The currencies of Argentina and Brazil are likely to keep their value in the face of rising U.S. interest rates, experts said.
The value of the Argentine peso hinges entirely on the credibility of the currency board, which Argentine leaders, regardless of their political stripes, are firmly committed to, they said.
Because of the currency, Argentine short rates will rise with U.S. rates, said Morgan Stanley's Brown. "The currency is safe, but asset values will be hit hardest."
In Brazil, tight monetary policy implies a strong and stable currency, experts say.

But the country's huge current account deficit makes the economy highly vulnerable to foreign capital flow, said Molano, who estimates that half of Brazil's $32 billion current account deficit is financed by foreign direct investment and the rest by portfolio investment.
Brazil has to raise interest rates more to match a rise in U.S. rates, if U.S. monetary policy changes, he said.
Molano does not expect a knock-on effect to Latin currencies if one buckles under the strain because trade integration in the region is low -- about 15 to 20 percent.
"Whatever correlation they have with each is due to their link with the U.S. dollar," he said.
